dedupe_keys.name: climate adapted restoration of the holla church ruins ulefoss norway climate adapt

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study documents the restoration of the medieval Holla church ruin at Ulefoss in south-eastern Norway to withstand more intense rainfall and more freeze-thaw cycles. Led by Riksantikvaren, the Norwegian Directorate for Cultural Heritage, with the Norwegian Society for Protection of Ancient Monuments and Holla municipality, the works replaced 1920s concrete joints with hydraulic lime, which tolerates moisture and weathering in an unroofed ruin; replaced slate wall caps with cast fibre-reinforced concrete slabs that slide on the wall tops so the walls do not crack as ground conditions change; swapped the soil within 25 cm of the walls for gravel to keep rainwater off them in wet periods and fire away in dry ones; and planted native species against erosion. A path and interpretation made the site accessible. The project ran from 2002 to 2020 and cost NOK 14.5 million, about EUR 1.4 million, including NOK 2.8 million in private donations; the works should stand for 100 years with monitoring and maintenance. Coverage: one heritage site. Access: the case study page, published on 28 February 2025 and modified on 25 August 2026, with Riksantikvaren's page in Norwegian. Licence: Climate-ADAPT content under the EEA reuse policy; free. Caveats: performance is expected, not measured, and the page gives no monitoring data. Simulation uses are a reference for moisture and frost damage mitigation on masonry in heritage risk models. Related records: the ReSCULT cultural heritage database record.
